gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured usable figure for any candidate. Side by side, OutdoorGearLab measured 870 Wh (85%) from the EcoFlow DELTA 3, 880 Wh (86%) from the DJI Power 1000 V2 and 950 Wh (82%) from the BLUETTI AC180, and StorageReview measured 910 Wh (88.9%) from the DELTA 3 Plus.
standout_why: I opened four of the rival pages: StormWatts (rank 1–2 in all chats, cited), offgridfieldguide.com (cited), WattHourLab (cited) and powerstationpilot was not opened. All three opened pages say outright that they did not test anything. StormWatts says 'We have not tested these products hands-on'. Off Grid Field Guide says 'We have not hands-on tested these units' and only assumes 'roughly 85 percent' reaches the outlet. WattHourLab uses spec-sheet figures only. thiswatt.com would not load (SSL error). None of them has a named measurement or a figure for a station running with its extra battery attached.
decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. The DELTA 3 (870 Wh measured) and DELTA 3 Plus (910 Wh measured) deliver as much as the DJI Power 1000 V2 (880 Wh) or more, so starting with EcoFlow costs no usable energy. The AC180's 950 Wh beats them on the base unit, but its add-on storage goes through the DC input rather than a battery port. A shopper should plan on roughly 85–89% of the rated Wh at the AC outlets, so 1,024 Wh plus a 1,024 Wh pack is about 1.75–1.8 kWh at the outlets. That is our arithmetic from the base-unit figures; nobody measured a station with its pack attached. The only expansion-specific measurement is from The Drive: the original DJI Power 1000 charged at up to 1,429 W with its Expansion Battery 2000 attached, against 960 W alone. Adding a pack can therefore change charge speed, not only capacity.
